clue.text: Stripper unable to find way to entertain copper

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to take them in, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: someone unable to find their way is lost
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A lost striptease artist lets a police officer into the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripper' suggests a dancer, but it is the insect that strips crops bare; 'copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Swarms of these insects strip fields of every leaf, so the creature is a stripper of vegetation.

clue.text: Powerful urge beginning to lessen, I offer nothing

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only the start of lessen is used

parts.note: to bid is to make an offer, as at an auction
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone tries to curb a strong craving by giving up everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Libido is sexual drive, a strong instinctive desire, so it is a powerful urge.

clue.text: Number of stars misbehaving, so I cannot tell

indicators.note: letters that misbehave do not stay in their places, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they cannot pick out which group of film stars is behaving badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misbehaving' rearranges the thirteen letters of 'so I cannot tell'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouping of stars forming a named pattern in the sky, such as Orion, is a number of stars together.

clue.text: Mailer securing stamp finally, one using money

indicators.note: securing something means holding it fast within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a mailer is one who sends post, a sender

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of stamp

explanation.surface: Someone posting a letter makes sure it carries a stamp, at a cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mailer' might suggest Norman Mailer, the American novelist, but it is simply one who mails.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lays out cash is a spender, one whose habit is using money.

clue.text: Crazy capital of Rajasthan, as old Indian city

parts.note: crazy means mad

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first, capital letter, so only the start of Rajasthan is used

explanation.surface: A traveller calls the capital of an Indian state crazy, likening it to another old city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital of Rajasthan' tempts you to think of Jaipur, but it just gives the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Madras was the former name of Chennai, a city on India's south-east coast, renamed in 1996.

clue.text: Greek author writing a page about European leader thus

indicators.note: about means around, so the first pair of letters goes round the others
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of European is used

parts.note: so means thus, in that way

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek writer fills a page about a European leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek storyteller credited with the fables, so he is a Greek author.

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, the first letter of relationship

parts.note: evolutionary describes gradual development

explanation.surface: A fresh romance is just starting to grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like an anagram signal, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something radically innovative that overturns the old ways can be called revolutionary, entirely new.

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a vestibule is an entrance hall, an entry

explanation.surface: A sentry posted in a cramped lobby.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier posted to keep watch at a gate or door is a guard on duty.

clue.text: Most thin — bet son struggling to eat infinitesimal starter

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other
struggling suggests a disordered thrashing about, so these letters are rearranged
a starter comes first, the opening letter of infinitesimal

explanation.surface: A gambler bets his skinny son can't manage a tiny starter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' rearranges BETSON into BONEST, and 'to eat' puts I, the start of 'infinitesimal', inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of bony, so the skinniest, with bones showing most through the skin.

clue.text: Street cop in disguise — that's confidential

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An undercover police officer on the beat insists the operation stays secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Highly classified information kept from all but a few is confidential in the strongest sense.

parts.note: two is divisible by two, so it is an even number

explanation.surface: Someone observes that the second number, two, is a certain kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven is a counting figure, one more than six, so it is a number.

parts.note: DA is a District Attorney, an American prosecutor
Ted is a man's name, standing for any bloke

explanation.surface: A lawyer is described as an old-fashioned man.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has gone out of style looks of its time, old-fashioned, behind the times.

indicators.note: inspiring is read as breathing in, taking a letter inside

parts.note: the poplar is a tall, fast-growing tree

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, the last letter of you

explanation.surface: A cherished tree that inspires someone in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inspiring' looks like praise, but it means breathing in: POPLAR takes in U.
explanation.definitionFit: Widely liked and admired, a favourite with many people, is the sense of much-loved.

indicators.note: making something new changes its form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A thief makes off with brand-new woodwind instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the legal term for theft, so one who commits it is a thief.

clue.text: Huge — a tenth of a centimetre seen differently

parts.note: a tenth of a centimetre is one millimetre, written I (one) and MM

indicators.note: differently means arranged another way, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tiny measurement looks vast when viewed in another way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface contrasts the tiny with the huge; 'a' gives I as the Roman numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immense is enormous, of vast size or extent, the same as huge.

clue.text: Burn disc, or char a little

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Damage a disc, or char it slightly, as with a hot iron.
explanation.definitionFit: To scorch is to burn a surface lightly, singeing or searing it.

parts.note: to cut off is to sever

explanation.surface: A northern river has been cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: The Severn is Britain's longest river, running from Wales through western England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn flows from mid-Wales to the Bristol Channel, Britain's longest waterway.

definitions.meaning: a thin, crisp, dry biscuit, often eaten with cheese
an informal British word for something excellent, as in a real corker

explanation.surface: Someone praises a biscuit as something marvellous.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a dry savoury biscuit, and British slang for a great example of something.

indicators.note: asking what was said points to the spoken sound of a word

parts.note: Neil is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A dog owner orders their pet to get down, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get down boy' reads as a command to a dog, but 'boy' is a name and 'Get down' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To go down on one's knees, as in church or before royalty, is to get down.

indicators.note: reportedly signals a word heard said rather than seen written

parts.note: a mousse is a light, airy dessert, a sweet in British usage

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have heard of a cute animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet' looks like an adjective for the animal, but it is a dessert, as the British call a pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: The moose is the largest member of the deer family, a large North American animal.

clue.text: River rising high in northern Europe, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter of each of these words is used

explanation.surface: A river runs high and rising in the north of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhine is a major European river flowing from the Alps through Germany to the North Sea.

indicators.note: putting one thing somewhere places it, here inside another piece
in says one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: tone means mood or atmosphere
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A trainer adjusts a horse's weight to put it in a good temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonnage is a measure of weight or capacity, usually of ships or cargo.

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: George Frideric Handel was the composer of Messiah

explanation.surface: Someone copes with the music of a great composer.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage or cope with a situation is to deal with it.

indicators.note: hugged by means held inside these words, the letters running across them

explanation.surface: An African visitor is embraced by an inebriated American.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Kenya, in East Africa, is an African.
